clue.text: Mark, comedian, probable loser?

blocks.note: a scratch is a mark on a surface
a card is an amusing, eccentric person, a joker

explanation.surface: A comedian named Mark is tipped to lose, perhaps at an awards night.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is playful: most of these lottery tickets win nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: An instant lottery ticket you rub to reveal a prize usually pays out nothing, so it is a likely dud purchase.

clue.text: Refurbishment of loos etc, most sophisticated

indicators.note: refurbishing something means rebuilding it, so the letters that follow are put together anew

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bathroom makeover turns the toilets into the smartest rooms in the house.
explanation.walkthrough: Loos is British slang for toilets.
explanation.definitionFit: Cool means stylish or fashionable in a polished way, so its superlative describes the most urbane and chic.

clue.text: More than one starter in tapas cooked with it

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A menu note: a mixed plate of appetisers makes up part of the tapas spread.
explanation.walkthrough: The food surface hides the fact that 'in tapas' and 'it' are all raw letters for the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian appetisers served before the main meal; the word is plural, matching the several dishes implied.

clue.text: Design boats

blocks.note: first meaning: to make or fashion something with skill
second meaning: vessels, a plural use of the same word

explanation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase it sounds like a naval architect's job; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to fashion skilfully; as a noun it is used, unchanged in the plural, for vessels.

clue.text: Old ships, clippers

blocks.note: first meaning: small fast single-masted sailing vessels
second meaning: tools for snipping, like shears

explanation.walkthrough: Clippers were also fast sailing ships, so the surface seems to give two names for vessels; the second is really the tool.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun names both fast sailing vessels of the past and implements used for snipping or trimming.

clue.text: Recover or collapse, finally, after period of relaxation

indicators.note: after places what follows behind the earlier pieces in the word order
finally points to the very end of the word it follows, keeping only its closing letter

blocks.note: a rest is a spell of relaxing
taken as written
the last letter of collapse

explanation.surface: Advice for the exhausted: after some downtime you will either bounce back or keel over.
explanation.definitionFit: To get back something lost, or bring it back to a former condition, is a common synonym sense.

clue.text: Brief during political campaign the pits, slow unfortunately

indicators.note: something gone unfortunately has gone wrong, so the letters before it fall out of their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A campaign trail moan: the tour is dreadful and painfully slow.
explanation.walkthrough: A whistle-stop tour, named after trains that halted at small stations, is a fast series of short campaign visits.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes a hurried tour of very short stops, the classic electioneering style of visiting many towns quickly.

clue.text: Seams, as broken by cutting upward

indicators.note: in a down clue, going upward means reading the word from bottom to top
a word broken by another is split open so the other can sit inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
a cutting remark is tart, sharp and biting

explanation.surface: Geology: rock layers fractured by digging upward through them.
explanation.definitionFit: Seams of coal or rock are layers in the ground, and strata is the geologist's plural for such layers.

clue.text: Result of stepping into boiling water in haste

definitions.text: Result of stepping into boiling water

blocks.clueFragment: Result of stepping into boiling water
blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: a scalded extremity
second meaning: rapidly, as an adverb

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a literal joke: put your foot in very hot water and that is what you get.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adverb, the word means quickly and eagerly, as when someone rushes off somewhere.

clue.text: Prove where cricket fan might be found?

definitions.text: where cricket fan might be found?
definitions.note: read as the two words AT TEST, a location

blocks.note: first meaning: to bear witness that something is true

blocks.clueFragment: where cricket fan might be found?
blocks.note: second meaning, split in two: present at a Test match

explanation.walkthrough: A Test is an international cricket match, so a fan could be at one; the answer split in two says just that.
explanation.definitionFit: To give evidence or certify that something is genuine is to demonstrate its truth, the same sense as proving.

clue.text: A little regular cash kept economy moving

indicators.note: moving sets the letters before it in motion, so they shift into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A modest steady income kept the household budget ticking over.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain this is the small weekly allowance parents give children.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a small weekly allowance, usually given to children, so a modest sum handed over routinely.

clue.text: Sea change, as fish enters drink

indicators.note: something that enters goes inside, so one word is placed within another

blocks.note: to sup is to drink, sip
the hake is a food fish

explanation.surface: A fish swimming into a drink suggests a sea creature in the wrong element.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea change is a radical transformation, and a dramatic reorganisation is the same idea.

clue.text: Lot more shaky — this sound?

indicators.note: a shaky thing is unsteady, so the letters before it are jiggled out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A singer is told to be much more wobbly, and asks if this is the effect wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This sound' points back at shakiness: the answer is a sound that wavers.
explanation.definitionFit: In music it is a wavering effect made by rapid repetition or fluctuation in pitch, a trembling tone.

clue.text: Minimum energy put in at the end

indicators.note: put in means placed inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: last means at the end, final
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone gives the least effort possible, only trying at the very end.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words express the smallest possible amount, as in the phrase at the very least.

clue.text: Nothing in paste’s OK when spread, as it were

indicators.note: in places the preceding word inside the one that follows
spreading something smears it about, so the letters are scattered into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written, with the apostrophe dropped
O looks like zero, nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A kitchen reassurance: the paste is fine with nothing in it once it is spread.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are fillers used to flag that one is speaking figuratively or loosely rather than literally.

clue.text: Get out and go on long walk

blocks.note: first meaning: a rude dismissal, go away
second meaning, literal: set off on a ramble

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like an invitation to a ramble; one meaning is an idiom telling someone to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a curt way of telling someone to clear off, while read literally it means setting out hiking.

clue.text: Comedy hit gets criticism

blocks.note: a slap is a hit with the open hand
stick is informal British for criticism, as in 'taking stick'

explanation.surface: A comedy show is a smash but the reviewers pan it.
explanation.walkthrough: To get stick is British slang for being criticised.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the knockabout physical style of humour full of pratfalls and custard pies.

clue.text: Style in embroidery of red coat

indicators.note: embroidery works threads into elaborate new patterns, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fashion note on the stitching style of a red jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the geometric decorative design movement of the 1920s and 1930s, an artistic manner of ornament.

clue.text: Sovereign for fruit?

blocks.note: first meaning: a female ruler, or the wife of a ruler, in a Muslim state
second meaning: a dried seedless grape

explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign is also an old gold coin, so the surface seems to ask about paying for fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a Muslim queen or a ruler's consort, and also a dried pale seedless grape used in baking.

clue.text: Make minimal effort while in bed

indicators.note: in puts the preceding word inside the one after it

blocks.note: a cot is a small bed
as can mean while, during the time that

explanation.surface: Doing as little as possible while lying in bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To freewheel without pedalling or effort is to proceed passively, getting by while trying as little as one can.

clue.text: Cheerful person carving block?

blocks.note: first meaning: lively and in good spirits
second meaning, playful: one who chips away at wood or stone

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the invented sense: someone who chips is, jokily, one who does that.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means bright and lively in spirits; as a playful noun it names whoever chips at material.

clue.text: Shocking gash in skin of adult, horrified

indicators.note: shocking upsets things, so the following word is jolted into a new order
the skin of a word is its outside, so only its first and last letters stay
in places the jumbled word inside the selected outer letters

blocks.note: the outer letters of adult
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A grown-up sees a nasty cut in the skin and recoils in horror.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone filled with sudden shock and dismay at something dreadful.

clue.text: Better off with freedom of movement

blocks.note: off and out both mean away, not in place, as a light that is off or out
play is slack, room to move, as in a rope

explanation.surface: Someone is happier now they are free to move about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better off' reads as one phrase, but 'Better' is the verb definition and 'off' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to better an opponent is to beat them, and to outplay is to perform more skilfully than a rival.

clue.text: Give in all that’s harvested

blocks.note: first meaning: surrender, submit
second meaning: the total crop produced

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests handing over a whole crop, but the two halves are separate senses.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to surrender or concede; as a noun it is the total amount of crop a field produces.

clue.text: Sneeze: and what I need for it when heard?

indicators.note: when heard means we go by how the words sound, not how they are written

blocks.note: a tissue is what one wants for a sneeze

explanation.surface: Someone sneezes and asks what they need to deal with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The spelling is the British way of writing a sneeze, the equivalent of achoo.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the written representation of the noise made when sneezing, an onomatopoeic interjection.

clue.text: People, terrific threat

blocks.note: men are people
ace means excellent, terrific

explanation.surface: People are told of a terrible danger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrific' seems to mean terrifying here, beside threat, but it is used in its sense of excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns name a person or thing likely to cause harm or danger.

clue.text: Yours truly is no longer popular, there’s no escaping it

blocks.note: yours truly is the setter, so 'yours truly is' becomes I'M
passé means out of fashion

explanation.surface: A setter confesses they are out of fashion, and there is no getting away from that fact.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadlock is a situation from which there is no way forward or out, which the clue phrases descriptively.

clue.text: Country music player in Terence animated old show

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the name that follows

blocks.note: Terry is a short form of the name Terence
Oman is a country on the Arabian Peninsula
a DJ, or disc jockey, plays records

explanation.surface: A country singer performs in a man called Terence's lively old show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country music' looks like one phrase, but it is a country and then a music player.
explanation.definitionFit: The classic cat-and-mouse cartoon series, first made in the 1940s, is a vintage animated programme.
